item.title: SCP Concept: Reflection: Re: SCP Concept: Reflection
item.content:encoded:
Once again, I thank you all for your feedbacks and I'll post this to you because I think you misunderstood the story a bit. Your whole understanding of this SCP is that it's main anomaly, the mirror, makes the individual's reflection possess the real one and make them commit suicide. This isn't really the case with my concept, my general idea and main focus of this is mostly the mirror because instead of it possessing the individual it manipulates them by turning the real individual into the reflection, thus making them follow the other's movement, so in general it just turns the person into the reflection sending them temporarily into a mirror dimension. They only die because by being the reflection itself if the mirror breaks the person dies with it and even tho the SCP kind of swaps places with the person it can't actually escape into the real world and will still be kept in the mirror. The gas station is simply a place where the main anomaly is stored, so that people who are on the road or passing by can take a quick break and go in there, which leads to their deaths.

(This will probably be the last reply I do so the posts aren't flooded with questions and answers)

item.title: Phantom Entry: Re: Phantom Entry
item.content:encoded:
Oh my, thank you for the response!

So to begin with, this is not really like, an "anti meme" kind of "anti meme". It's a piece of entry in the database, perfectly readable, perfectly manipulatable, but the content DESCRIBES it as an anti meme, with the help of the entity claiming that it is. The actual entry itself isn't antimemetic, the content only CLAIMS that it is. This happens because documentation happens side by side with research, as requested by the entity because it is sating our curiosity to its amusement. Then after it departed, everyone involved instantly forgets everything and has each of their "unreadable" memory filled with vague fabrications, but the SCP entry remains, fully authorized and reviewed even. Hence, the "anomality" of the situation, where the containment procedure is supposed to be executed, none of the staff mentioned in the entry responded, resulting in disciplinary actions, but then turning into an immediate confusion fiesta where no one remembers about it, resulting in the proposal that the entry is anomalous.

Remember, this SCP is not really all just about the content of the anomalous entry, it's also about the validity of the entry, as it's at the end of the day just another documentation, only with no evidence. So this could be an anomaly in the system, maybe a security overlook and some rando messed with the database, possible sabotage, drunk researcher, who knows?

In the entry, the foundation really doesn't do much but interviews at first, since the entity creates the first impression of being another reluctant reality hopper, hence being treated as such. Standard Humanoid chamber, all that stuff. Each entry, the foundation catches it roaming more and more, sometimes suddenly in other SCP chambers, disappear from its own the room, interacting more and more to the point of making people uncomfortable and disturbed. Every time it does questionable things, it gets hit with another interview, and as the entry goes on this cycle will get deeper and deeper as it straight up appears in Keter facilities, roam outside of the protected area, "accidentally" causing a breach, speaks more aggressively, lose its charming attitude, etc etc. Basically, it's character changes questionably each passing day, and the foundation will be conflicted to take action as each misbehavioural instance caused no casualty, but is still dangerous until it goes so severe the foundation gets extremely desperate (where it gets a Keter label and is clearly uncontainable), and at the peak of mass panic, the entity settles down, reveals what it has been up to which is a research of its own, and went adios. There ends the entry.

But again, very important to note that this is an SCP entry about an SCP entry, which plays a huge part in the informational horror element, as viewers as left with a lot of doubt and questions regarding the entry. The actual, non-content entry will be very passive and boring because it really is just about a random documentation with no proof but is able to have so much authenticity in written permission, authorization, all the legal shenanigans. It basically will have weird pacing that kicks the readers in the end, saying "hey maybe all of that was lie lol".

item.title: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights): Re: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for your review. It's very informative.

Indeed, I omitted to present my ideas to build around this SCP, due to wanting to be very thorough with its description.

The article would describe the SCP in the usual objective fashion, complemented with tests to understand its properties :

For example, a log could feature uncomfortable D-classes eating through all sorts of food to test out which trigger teeth apparitions, and subsequently get diagnosed with some bone disease. Then, the article would show studies made about the transmutation, trying to understand exactly what kind of objects gets transmuted (do regular teeth also work?)

The article itself will describe the object's known properties thoroughly and the reader may make the rapprochement with the tooth fairy (but whether they do or do not is not very important).

I think this is enough to make a short article about a fun weird object that is at the same time somewhat cute (turning your fallen teeth into a small payment) and somewhat unsettling (teeth in your food, osteoporosis and radiations). What do you think?

item.title: Night Terrors - Seeking Idea Critique: Re: Night Terrors - Seeking Idea Critique
item.content:encoded:
I get like, the child manifesting horrors to protect herself from nightmares but my concern here is it feels weird to mix like…dream terrors with real protection? Like, why doesn't she create dream monsters that exist solely in her dreams to protect her? Obviously that wouldn't really be a SCP then but it feels…weird

I can see how that would feel weird! I should have been more specific but I was trying not to ramble on. I established that the child has C-PTSD, but I should have been more clear as to why.

I've loosely based the manifestation of her anomaly on "An American Haunting," if you've ever seen it. The narratives of the two children are quite different, but their situations are very similar. It's an incredibly heavy topic, and I want to make sure I write it respectfully.

The neglect by her mother, and unspeakable abuse by her father has caused the child to live her formative years in a near constant state of fear, and panic. Repeated physical, emotional, and sexual abuse she is unable to comprehend led to these frequent nightmares. After some time, her suffering was so intense that she began to lose herself in the nightmares, because they were less terrifying than her real life. Those nightmares then became a shield for her, and eventually a literal weapon.

Also if the monsters are protecting her, why are they hostile to all lifeforms (which might be a bit broad btw, like SCP-3749 shows, 'all lifeforms' includes 'bacteria' of which there are thousands in the air) and not just like, hostile lifeforms? Or even unknown lifeforms: it feels like if e.g. her mother approached, they wouldn't attack?

Oh wow, I hadn't even considered just how broad that could be. I suppose to be more specific I should condense it down to humanoid lifeforms and entities. Thank you for pointing that out!

As far as why it attacks all (decidedly humanoid) lifeforms, in my head she's been through so much struggle and pain at such a young age, especially by those who were meant to protect her, her brain perceives all beings other than herself a potential threat. While the child usually chooses flight mode, her monsters always choose fight.

So like, narratively what does this actually look like? My concern is that it feels like it could be very passive, but also like it might not be that interesting to read? It really depends on how this conflict plays out and stuff.

That is my biggest fear - that it wont be interesting to read. My idea was to narrate the process and discovery of her origin through incident reports, interview logs, addendums and such, while trying to make it concise enough to be reasonably palatable. My goal is make the readers feel sympathy for the child, while reasonably portraying The Foundation and the interactions between them.

Thank you so much for responding by the way! I appreciate it greatly.

item.title: Seeking Greenlights: My Eyes are Up Here: Re: Seeking Greenlights: My Eyes are Up Here
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for the clarification. Now that I'm clear on your intentions, I can offer a bit of crit.

+ Collapsing this as to save space
fwoop

I want to note that, in many ways, the subject matter is still uncomfortable. Even as I now understand your desire to make this an anti-harassment story, an anomaly based on the objectification of a woman's breasts is practically a minefield for things to go wrong.

I don't mean to say that you can't write this in a way that is respectful, it's just moreso to do with the subject matter itself. Sexual harassment, in general, is a dubious1 topic to write about. Once again, your intentions are essentially irrelevant if you can't articulate them in a way that gets them across clearly. (In this case, misinterpretation is a killer.)

Now, I'd like to touch on the actual story itself, setting aside my previous concerns for a moment. In particular, I'd like to get a bit more insight into the structure. I largely hold that the way you portray your narrative holds just as much, if not more importance than the narrative itself. (See also: the initial points in this posts. They link together quite well.)

From my understanding, there is an initial incident regarding Dr. Briggs that ends in his blindness. Following that, experimentation on Lopez. I understand that the initial incident serves the narrative purpose of introducing the anomaly while also giving the "pervert gets what he deserves" point, which is fine. I'm still largely unclear on the experiments, which really should serve some sort of narrative purpose. Are they going to make a nuanced point on anti-harassment? Or are they just going to serve as an explanation for how the anomaly works? I should note that the latter generally just… isn't interesting. A reader could care less about the inner semantics of an anomaly. An SCP article is a narrative that follows a specific format - if you end a story on "and THIS is how is all happened…", it's generally going to feel weak.

based on an interview with Lopez's parents, it is speculated that it might have first come about during puberty.

This seems to be another addition? Many of my points above apply here - what do you think this would add, would the reader really care about this? Would its inclusion benefit the article, or would it only serve as unnecessary bloat? As an aside, what do you hope to achieve with this point? Is it a subtle protest against the objectification of young women? It might be the lack of context, but the point as it stands is just… creepy.

Footnotes
1. I'm using this term very liberally.
